word:hebrew:H1030.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Beth” or “Bethshemite.” It identifies a person or designation connected with Beth in the two recorded passages in 1 Samuel 6. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within that chapter. Because no broader definition or verse text is available here, its precise role depends on the surrounding wording; its supported sense is the name or Beth-related designation preserved by these renderings.

word:hebrew:H107.explanation: Iggereth means an epistle or letter, a written message sent from one person or group to another.

word:hebrew:H1085.explanation: Bildad is the name of one of Job’s friends.

word:hebrew:H1122.explanation: Ben is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H1157.explanation: Be'ad can mean up to, against, or for. It marks direction in going up to Yahweh, and it can also mean for, as when Moses prayed for the people.

word:hebrew:H1236.explanation: Biq'ah means a plain. It can describe the place where an image was set up.

word:hebrew:H1269.explanation: Birzavith is a Hebrew name, functioning primarily to identify someone rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. Its meaning in the biblical text is therefore tied to the person or name it designates, not to an ordinary English concept. This word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both counted at 1 Chronicles 7:31. The available rendering, “Birzavith,” preserves it as a name rather than translating it into a descriptive term.

word:hebrew:H1315.explanation: Bashemath is a personal name, rendered “Bashemath.” It identifies a woman in Old Testament genealogical and family records rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible corpus, chiefly in Genesis and once in 1 Kings. Its uses are connected with family relationships and genealogical listings, including records concerning marriage and descent. Because no broader lexical definition is provided, its ordinary meaning here is its function as a woman’s name: it identifies the person named Bashemath. [evidence IDs]

word:hebrew:H1478.explanation: Gava means to expire, that is, to die.

word:hebrew:H1492.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “fleece,” referring to the woolly covering taken from a sheep. It occurs seven times in the Old Testament, all within Judges 6:37–40. In its recorded uses, it functions as the object being spoken about or requested, especially in speech involving a sign. The word therefore identifies a physical fleece, while the surrounding words determine what is being said or asked about it.

word:hebrew:H1571.explanation: Gam means also, marking an addition to what has already been mentioned. It can also mean again when an event is repeated.

word:hebrew:H1614.explanation: Gophrith means sulfur, also called brimstone.

word:hebrew:H172.explanation: Aholibah is a personal name, referring to a woman in Ezekiel’s prophetic message. It is not presented here as a general Hebrew word describing an object, action, or quality. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all within Ezekiel 23. Scripture associates Aholibah with family identity and genealogy, and repeatedly treats her as the object of speech and other actions in the passage. The precise significance of the name in each verse depends on the surrounding text.

word:hebrew:H1816.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to inflammation, a burning or inflamed condition affecting the body. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 28:22. As a noun, it names a physical ailment rather than an action or person. The available rendering pattern supports “inflammation” as its clearest ordinary meaning. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a painful bodily condition marked by heat, irritation, or swelling.

word:hebrew:H1849.explanation: Dâphaq means to knock. It can also mean to press severely, as when flocks are overdriven.

word:hebrew:H1975.explanation: Hallaz means this or that, pointing to a person or thing in view.

word:hebrew:H198.explanation: Ulam is a personal name borne by two Israelites.

word:hebrew:H2080.explanation: Zebidah is a personal name used for an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. Its rendered form is "Zebidah," and it functions as a name, not as a common description or action word. It appears twice in one verse, 2 Kings 23:36, making it a very rare personal designation. As with other names, its precise reference is determined by the surrounding sentence and context.

word:hebrew:H2101.explanation: Zôwb means a discharge or flow from the body. It can describe a man's running discharge or a woman's blood discharge that continues beyond her period.

word:hebrew:H2233.explanation: Zera means seed. It can also refer to offspring or descendants.

word:hebrew:H2291.explanation: Haggi is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. It appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across two verses, and is consistently rendered “Haggi.” The name occurs in Genesis 46:16 and Numbers 26:15. Those references establish where the name appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the role of the named person in each passage.

word:hebrew:H2439.explanation: Chiysh means to hurry or make haste.

word:hebrew:H2466.explanation: Heled is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Heled” in English. It does not have an explicit descriptive definition in the available lexical information, so its ordinary use here is as a name identifying an individual. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 11:30. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, which are not included here.

word:hebrew:H2484.explanation: Chelyah means a trinket. In its recorded usage, it refers to a jewel.

word:hebrew:H2563.explanation: Chomer means clay or a heap, and it can also name a dry measure.

word:hebrew:H2637.explanation: Chaser means to lack or become less.

word:hebrew:H2642.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to a condition described as “wanting”—something is lacking or incomplete. It functions as a name for that condition rather than as an action or command. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ecclesiastes 1:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense points to deficiency: something cannot be made complete because something is missing.

word:hebrew:H2710.explanation: Chaqaq means to engrave or inscribe.

word:hebrew:H275.explanation: Ahuzam is a personal name, referring to a man named in the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs only once, in 1 Chronicles 4:6, within a genealogical record. The available rendering identifies him as “Ahuzam,” so the word functions as a name rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance beyond identifying this person is not stated in the available passage evidence.

word:hebrew:H28.explanation: Abida is a personal name, rendered “Abida” in this Hebrew Old Testament data. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its basic role is to name a person. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew corpus, in Genesis 25:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:33. Because no verse text or additional lexical definition is available here, the name’s precise significance cannot be stated beyond this naming function.

word:hebrew:H2817.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name, rendered “Hasupha.” It functions as a name rather than a common description or action. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. The English spelling varies slightly between those passages, but the word is identified with the same Hebrew entry. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding genealogical context of each passage.

word:hebrew:H2862.explanation: Chathaph means to clutch. It can also describe taking or snatching something away.

word:hebrew:H2888.explanation: Tabbath is a proper name identifying a particular place. This Hebrew word functions as a name rather than a general descriptive term, and it is rendered “Tabbath.” It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 7:22. Its main meaning is therefore identification: it distinguishes this named location from other places. The word itself does not express an action, quality, or broad concept. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H2945.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “little,” meaning young or small members of a group, especially children. It functions as a designation for those viewed as young or dependent rather than as mature adults. In the Old Testament, it occurs 42 times and is used in settings involving families, communities, travel, warfare, and the wider people of Israel. Its use can include children among those counted, protected, carried, or affected by a community’s actions.

word:hebrew:H3054.explanation: Yahad means to become Jewish—to Judaize.

word:hebrew:H3120.explanation: Javan is a personal name. It can also refer to a people among the nations.

word:hebrew:H316.explanation: Aharhel is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:8. The available biblical usage presents it within a genealogy, so its role is to name an individual in that family record. Scripture does not provide an explicit definition for the name, and its precise name-meaning should therefore not be expanded beyond this identified usage.

word:hebrew:H3195.explanation: Jetur is a Hebrew proper name rendered “Jetur.” It identifies a named person or people-group rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears three times in the Old Testament: once in Genesis and twice in 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, since the name itself functions primarily as an identifying designation.

word:hebrew:H3238.explanation: Yanah means to be violent and can also mean to oppress or maltreat.

word:hebrew:H3313.explanation: Yapha means to shine or shine forth.

word:hebrew:H349.explanation: Eyk means how, asking how something can happen or be done. It can also introduce an exclamation, as in “How the mighty have fallen!”

word:hebrew:H3568.explanation: Cush is a personal name. It can also name a territory rendered “Ethiopia” in some English translations.

word:hebrew:H3582.explanation: Kachad means to hide or conceal; it can also mean to cut off or destroy.

word:hebrew:H3612.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name Caleb, a man identified throughout the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. Caleb appears in Israel’s wilderness history and later in genealogical records, so the name occurs across both narrative and family-list passages. The Hebrew corpus contains 35 occurrences, all in the Old Testament. Scripture identifies him repeatedly among Israel’s people, including references in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and later genealogies.

word:hebrew:H3667.explanation: This Hebrew word means “Canaan,” the proper name used for the land and people associated with Canaan in the Old Testament. It functions as a place or people designation rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs 94 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Genesis and the books describing Israel’s journey, settlement, and inheritance. Its precise reference—land, people, or territorial setting—comes from the surrounding sentence.

word:hebrew:H3726.explanation: This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Ammoni,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Joshua 18:24. As a name, it identifies the particular named entity referred to by the text. No further English definition is established here, so its precise identity and significance must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from this word alone.

word:hebrew:H3779.explanation: Kasday means a Chaldean, an inhabitant of Chaldaea. It can also refer to a professional astrologer.

word:hebrew:H3887.explanation: Luwts means to mock or scorn. It can also refer to an interpreter.

word:hebrew:H4068.explanation: Madon is a place name in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H4082.explanation: Medinah means a district or province, a region under jurisdiction.

word:hebrew:H4165.explanation: Mûwtsâq means a casting. It can also describe material hardened into a mass.

word:hebrew:H419.explanation: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Eldad.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general term describing an object, action, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 11:26–27, and English renderings preserve it as “Eldad.” The surrounding SEE evidence places the name in a speech-related setting and connects it with a person, but the word itself identifies the individual rather than expressing the content or significance of what was said.

word:hebrew:H4226.explanation: Mechabberah means a coupling or joining piece, such as a brace or cramp.

word:hebrew:H4279.explanation: Machar means tomorrow, the following day. It can also refer more broadly to time to come or hereafter.

word:hebrew:H4312.explanation: Medad is a Hebrew personal name identifying a particular man, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a proper name: it points to the same individual wherever it appears. In the Hebrew Old Testament, Medad occurs twice, both times in Numbers 11:26–27. The surrounding SEE patterns associate the name with a person and with speech, but the name itself simply identifies Medad. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the actual passage context.

word:hebrew:H4367.explanation: Machnadebai is a personal name, rendered “Machnadebai.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:40, and both recorded English renderings preserve it as “Machnadebai.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name of the person identified in Ezra’s record.

word:hebrew:H4420.explanation: Melechah means barren land. It can also refer to salt land.

word:hebrew:H4495.explanation: Manoach is the name of an Israelite, rendered Manoah in English.

word:hebrew:H4554.explanation: This Hebrew word means “provender,” referring to supplies given to animals. It functions as a noun, naming something that can be brought, placed, or given as part of providing for animals. In its five Old Testament occurrences, it appears in scenes involving hospitality, travel, and the provision of animals, especially in Genesis. Its repeated connection with giving shows that the word identifies the provision itself rather than the action of supplying it.

word:hebrew:H4613.explanation: Moʻŏmâd means a foothold or standing, a place to stand.

word:hebrew:H4738.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to “divination,” the practice of seeking knowledge or guidance through supernatural means rather than through ordinary observation. It names the thing being discussed, not an action performed by the word itself. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel, where it is associated with claims made through speech. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:hebrew:H4811.explanation: Meraiah is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears once, in Nehemiah 12:12, and the English rendering preserves it as “Meraiah.” Because the available information identifies the word as a name but does not provide a separate lexical definition, its main function is to identify that individual by name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain his specific role there.

word:hebrew:H4932.explanation: Mishneh means second in order. It can also describe something double in amount. It can also mean a copy.

word:hebrew:H4947.explanation: This Hebrew word means “lintel,” the horizontal beam above a doorway. It names a physical part of a door entrance rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus 12, where it is associated with the doorway and with applying something to it. Its precise role in each sentence depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the upper beam of the entrance.

word:hebrew:H503.explanation: Alaph means to make a thousandfold, or to bring forth thousands.

word:hebrew:H5229.explanation: Nekochah describes what is right. It also describes equity or uprightness.

word:hebrew:H5276.explanation: Naem means to be agreeable or pleasant. It can also describe something sweet.

word:hebrew:H5294.explanation: Neariah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament, it appears three times, all in 1 Chronicles, and is rendered consistently as “Neariah.” The name occurs in genealogical or family-list settings, but the available word-level information does not establish a broader symbolic meaning or explain the individuals’ roles. Thus, its ordinary meaning for a Bible reader is simply the proper name Neariah, with the surrounding passage identifying which person is intended.

word:hebrew:H5355.explanation: Naqiy means innocent. It can also describe someone as guiltless or blameless. It can describe someone as clear from an oath.

word:hebrew:H5405.explanation: Nashath means to dry up or fail.

word:hebrew:H5548.explanation: Salcah is the name of a place east of the Jordan.

word:hebrew:H5661.explanation: Abdiel is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 5:15, and is rendered “Abdiel.” Because no lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the name itself is the clearest supported meaning. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic function is to identify a person.

word:hebrew:H5764.explanation: Uwl means an infant; it can also describe a sucking child.

word:hebrew:H5786.explanation: Avar means to blind. It can also describe putting out someone's eyes.

word:hebrew:H5823.explanation: ʻAzaq means to grub over and can also mean to fence about. In the vineyard picture, it is rendered “fenced.”

word:hebrew:H5881.explanation: Enan is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify an individual rather than express an action, quality, or object. In the Old Testament, it appears five times, all in Numbers, and is consistently rendered “Enan.” Because no explicit definition is given, the name’s meaning cannot be expanded beyond this identification. Its references range from Numbers 1 through Numbers 10, showing repeated mention within that book’s records.

word:hebrew:H5944.explanation: Aliyyah means an upper room or chamber.

word:hebrew:H6075.explanation: This Hebrew word describes acting on something as “presumed”—treating it as settled or certain rather than waiting for confirmation. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 14:44 and Habakkuk 2:4. Its use is uncommon, so the surrounding sentence is especially important for understanding the precise action being described. The word functions as an expression of a person’s confident assumption or bold response.

word:hebrew:H608.explanation: This Hebrew word is the pronoun “ye,” used to address the people being spoken to. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, at Daniel 2:8. Because it functions as a direct address, it points to the listeners or people being addressed rather than naming an object, place, or action. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

word:hebrew:H6116.explanation: Atserah means an assembly, especially one held for a festival or holiday. It can also describe a solemn assembly.

word:hebrew:H6149.explanation: ʻAreb means to be agreeable. It can also describe something as pleasant or sweet.

word:hebrew:H6251.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to “flocks,” specifically livestock spoken of as a group. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it appears in Deuteronomy and is connected with the increase, blessing, cursing, or consumption of flocks. The word functions as something that can be given, blessed, lost, or eaten, depending on the sentence. Its central sense remains a collective term for flocks rather than an action or quality.

word:hebrew:H6307.explanation: Paddan is a Hebrew geographical name, also rendered “Aram,” referring to the region associated with the patriarchal family’s journeys and marriages. It appears 21 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Genesis, and is used as a place designation rather than as a description of a person, action, or quality. The name is connected with references to going to, coming from, and living in that region, especially in accounts concerning Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and their families. Its exact force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H6372.explanation: Pinechas is a personal name, rendered Phinehas in English.

word:hebrew:H6398.explanation: Palach means to slice or cut something into pieces. It can also describe breaking something apart or piercing through it.

word:hebrew:H6408.explanation: Piltai is a Hebrew personal name. It identifies an individual rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nehemiah 12:17, and is rendered “Piltai” in the available English translations. Since no broader definition or descriptive meaning is supplied, its clearest significance is as the proper name of the person it identifies in that passage.

word:hebrew:H6497.explanation: This Hebrew noun refers to “knops,” a specific kind of object named in descriptions of the temple furnishings. It occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, all in 1 Kings: once in 1 Kings 6:18 and twice in 1 Kings 7:24. The word therefore functions as a concrete noun for these named objects rather than as an action, quality, or abstract idea. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the objects being described.

word:hebrew:H6534.explanation: Parmashta is a personal name in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies one individual and is rendered “Parmashta.” This word occurs only once in the Old Testament corpus, so its meaning is chiefly its role as that person’s name rather than a common term describing an action, quality, or object. Its recorded occurrence is Esther 9:9. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s place in that passage.

word:hebrew:H6589.explanation: Pasak means to open wide. It can also describe opening the feet.

word:hebrew:H6619.explanation: Pithom is a place name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus 1:11, and both recorded English renderings preserve it as “Pithom.” Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points readers to a particular location. The surrounding verse supplies the historical significance of that location, while the word itself names it.

word:hebrew:H6646.explanation: Tsᵉbîyâh means a female gazelle, also called a roe.

word:hebrew:H6703.explanation: Tsach means bright. It can describe something clear or plain. It can also describe something white.

word:hebrew:H6822.explanation: Tsaphah means to watch or observe. It can also describe waiting for something.

word:hebrew:H6857.explanation: Zephath is the name of a place in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a separately stated definition; its English rendering preserves the place name as “Zephath.” This Hebrew entity occurs once, in Judges 1:17. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies that location.

word:hebrew:H6930.explanation: Qadmonah means eastern or east, describing direction toward the east.

word:hebrew:H6985.explanation: This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 16:47. Because the surrounding verse and a fuller definition are needed to determine its precise force, it is best understood cautiously rather than expanded into several possible meanings. The word may describe a narrowly defined action, condition, or quality, but the reference alone does not establish which one. Its meaning must therefore be read from the complete sentence and surrounding passage.

word:hebrew:H7032.explanation: Qal means a sound or a voice.

word:hebrew:H7047.explanation: Qeles means a laughing-stock or derision.

word:hebrew:H7111.explanation: Ketsaphah means bark stripped from a tree.

word:hebrew:H7209.explanation: Rᵉʼîy means a mirror or looking glass.

word:hebrew:H7256.explanation: Ribbêaʻ refers to a descendant of the fourth generation, or a great-great-grandchild.

policy.priorReviewerNotes: LEX_DEF supports the meaning, but W2 directly supports mourning/restlessness rather than the exact claim that the word means to tramp about or ramble. “Disconsolate” is also unnecessarily obscure for a reader-facing explanation.

word:hebrew:H734.explanation: Orach means a well-trodden road or path, literally or figuratively. It can also refer figuratively to a person's way or manner. It may also refer to a caravan or troop.

word:hebrew:H7418.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to “Ramoth,” a place name. It is also rendered “south,” so its precise sense depends on how it functions in the sentence. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both within 1 Samuel 30:27. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the safest explanation is that it identifies Ramoth and may also express a southern location or direction in that passage. It is therefore best understood as a geographical term rather than a general description of a person, action, or spiritual quality.

word:hebrew:H7487.explanation: This Hebrew word means “flourishing.” It describes something as thriving and in a healthy, vigorous state, presenting a picture of prosperity and vitality rather than weakness or decline. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 4:4, so Scripture gives only a single recorded setting for this term. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is flourishing well-being.

word:hebrew:H7573.explanation: Ratham means to yoke up or bind a vehicle.

word:hebrew:H7641.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “ears,” referring to the grain-bearing heads of a plant. It is used in the Old Testament for visible ears of grain in agricultural or harvest imagery. The word occurs 19 times in 16 verses, so it has a focused meaning rather than a broad range of uses. In some passages, these ears are part of spoken descriptions or reports, showing that the word names a concrete feature of grain.

word:hebrew:H7704.explanation: Sadeh means a field or open ground. A field can be a place where someone hunts.

word:hebrew:H7865.explanation: Sion refers to the summit of Mount Hermon.

word:hebrew:H789.explanation: The Hebrew word refers to the Ashbelites, a people identified by that name. It functions as a group name rather than a description of an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Numbers 26:38. Since the verse text is not provided here, the word’s broader significance in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context.

word:hebrew:H7968.explanation: Shallun is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H8037.explanation: Shamma is the name of an Israelite.

word:hebrew:H8042.explanation: Semali means situated on the left side, describing a left hand or a pillar placed on the left.

word:hebrew:H8110.explanation: Shimron is the name of an Israelite. It also names a place in Palestine.

word:hebrew:H815.explanation: Eshel means a tamarisk tree and can also refer to a grove.

word:hebrew:H8239.explanation: Shaphath means to set something in place. It can also mean to bring something into a place.

word:hebrew:H8266.explanation: Shâqar means to cheat or be untrue, usually in words.

word:hebrew:H8284.explanation: Sharah means a fortification, literally or figuratively.

word:hebrew:H8363.explanation: Shethil means a plant or sprig.

word:hebrew:H8433.explanation: Tokhechah means chastisement or reproof. It can also refer to an argument presented in support of a case.

word:hebrew:H8491.explanation: This word means “Tizite”. It is a rare Hebrew word preserved as a proper identifying term rather than a commonly translated description. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 11:45, and English translations retain the same name-like rendering. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the passage must provide the specific significance of the person or place connected with it. Its basic meaning is therefore the identifying name “Tizite,” not a broader quality, action, or concept.

word:hebrew:H8635.explanation: This Hebrew word refers to an increase—something becoming greater in amount or extent. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 32:14. As a noun-like expression, it names the increase itself rather than describing an action. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains growth or added quantity. The word’s connection with related terms in that verse places it within language about something being increased or brought about in greater measure.

word:hebrew:H936.explanation: Bûwz means to disrespect or despise.

word:hebrew:H969.explanation: This Hebrew noun means “tower,” referring to a raised or fortified structure. It appears once in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Jeremiah 6:27. As a noun, it names the structure itself rather than an action or quality. The available scriptural reference identifies its occurrence, while the surrounding verse text is not included here, so its particular significance in that passage must be understood from the wider context of Jeremiah.
